items.title: livox_gz_sim: Livox Mid-360 and HAP simulation for Gazebo Harmonic
items.summary: Hi all, I’ve released livox_gz_sim, a Gazebo Harmonic plugin that simulates Livox Mid-360 and HAP lidars and publishes exactly what livox_ros_driver2 publishes. As far as I know it’s the first gpu agnostic Livox simulator for Gazebo Harmonic; the existing ones target Gazebo Classic or require CUDA. What it does Uses Livox’s recorded non-repetitive scan patterns, so coverage builds up over frames like on the real sensor Publishes livox_ros_driver2/CustomMsg or PointCloud2 in the driver’s 26-byte layout (xfer_format 0/1), with per-point timestamps Simulates the Mid-360’s IMU at 200 Hz Adds range and angle noise from the datasheet, and reflectivity (0–255) from <laser_retro> Supports multiple sensors, configurable publish rate and downsampling, and world resets Because the output matches the driver, stacks like FAST-LIO run on it unchanged. Repo: GitHub - mathaimp/livox_gz_sim: ROS2 Livox Lidar Simulation · GitHub Requires livox_ros_driver2 for the message types only, plus an OpenGL-capable GPU. Feedback, issues, and requests for other Livox models are welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic

items.articleText: A small deterministic gate between the planner and the wheels: ROS 2 Jazzy node, simulation and CI only - Projects - Open Robotics Discourse A small deterministic gate between the planner and the wheels: ROS 2 Jazzy node, simulation and CI only Projects ros2 , jazzy , supervisorygate marunigno-ship-it November 1, 2026, 11:04am 1 I’ve been building a small supervisor node for differential-drive mobile robots that sits between a high-level velocity source (such as Nav2, an LLM agent, or teleoperation) and the base controller. Following the classic Simplex architecture (Sha et al.), the node treats complex high-level planners as unverified proposers and acts as a minimal, deterministic gatekeeper on /cmd_vel. I work alone and I’m self-taught, based in Greece. I have no access to physical robot hardware, so everything described below is evaluated in Webots simulation (PAL Robotics TIAGo base) and verified in GitHub Actions Linux containers. I want to share what the node does, what the CI shows and doesn’t show, and the specific mistakes I made getting it through CI, in the hope it saves someone else an afternoon, or not What it is The package is qerra_core (node qerra_gate_node, version 0.3.0, Apache-2.0, ROS 2 Jazzy). It subscribes to /cmd_vel, /scan, and an operator reset topic, and publishes /cmd_vel_safe and diagnostic JSON on /gate/state. planner (Nav2, teleop, etc.) --/cmd_vel–> [ qerra_gate_node ] --/cmd_vel_safe–> base controller /scan ------^ distress input (UDP 5008) --^ The core decision logic is a pure function—step(state, params, inputs)—implemented using standard-library integer arithmetic with no external dependencies and with timestamps passed in as inputs. This design allows control cycles to be replayed and verified offline bit-for-bit. Key behaviors: Kinematic stopping envelope : Clamps wheel velocity commands against a swept forward lidar corridor: d_stop = ceil(v^2 / (2*a)) + ceil(v * t_react) + margin (where a = 0.5 m/s², t_react = 32 ms, margin = 300 mm). Fail-closed trips : Commands zero velocity and latches on obstacle breach, stale/invalid proposals (≥ 150 ms), sensor stalls, or acute distress telemetry. Calm dwell & operator reset : Once tripped, the robot remains stationary. Resuming motion strictly requires a continuous 1.0-second clear dwell window followed by an explicit operator reset message (/gate/reset). Reset is strictly refused while a hazard is present. Distress reflex input (Layer 1B) : Ingests non-blocking UDP telemetry (port 5008) inspired by ISO 13482 assistive cobot principles, tripping the gate on CRITICAL distress. (“HSR” in my documentation is my internal project name for this reflex layer and has no connection to Toyota’s robot). Node-level fault latch : If an unhandled exception occurs inside the 32 ms control tick, the node latches into a permanent FAULT state, continually publishes a zero velocity command, reports the fault reason over /gate/state, and refuses to move until the process is restarted. Topology note : The base controller is intended to be wired to /cmd_vel_safe, and nothing else should publish to it. ROS 2 topic namespaces do not enforce sole write authority. What I can show (The Evidence) Simulation replays : Webots runs logging each tick with a SHA-256 rolling hash chain that verifies offline via verify_log.py --replay. In Demo 7, an obstacle trip fired at 337 mm clearance, reaching standstill at 301 mm (36 mm coasting). In Demo 9, injected human distress tripped the gate within the same 32 ms tick (cycle 125), held standstill through dwell stabilization, and motion resumed only after an authorized reset. Native ROS 2 Jazzy CI (workflow file: QERRA-v2-classical/.github/workflows/ros2_jazzy.yml at main · marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical · GitHub Running on Ubuntu 24.04 in an official ros:jazzy container, GitHub Actions builds the package with colcon, verifies discovery in lib/qerra_core, starts the executable from a neutral directory (/tmp), captures a live /gate/state message, sends SIGINT, and strictly asserts that the process exits with code 0 and logs zero tick exceptions. What I cannot show (Honesty Boundaries) No hardware validation : Everything is simulation and CI. A 0.0 velocity command is a software setpoint delivered to motor drivers, not a certified hardware Safe Torque Off (STO), brake coil, or emergency stop. If the gate process dies, the base controller will maintain its last command unless the base has its own hardware or software command timeout. Timing and jitter : The node runs on a Python timer at 31.25 Hz on general-purpose Linux. I have not profiled execution jitter under heavy system load. Reaction time (t_react) : The 32 ms figure is a simulation assumption. On a real robot, total reaction latency includes physical sensor scan time (a Hokuyo URG-04LX operates at ~10 Hz / 100 ms), executor queueing, DDS transport, and motor deceleration ramps. Until measured, d_stop is likely optimistic for real hardware. Comparison with Nav2 : I have not benchmarked this against nav2_collision_monitor. nav2_collision_monitor is far more mature and feature-complete. My implementation is an exploration of Simplex state-latching, explicit calm dwells, and replayable pure-function cores. Standards are informative : References to ISO 13849-1, ISO 13482, and ISO 3691-4 are conceptual references only; no formal compliance is claimed. What went wrong in CI (Lessons Learned) Getting the standalone node to build, tick, and terminate cleanly under native Jazzy CI exposed five subtle issues: Missing setup.cfg : The console script was initially installed into bin/ rather than lib//, leaving ros2 pkg executables completely blank. Adding setup.cfg with explicit script directories fixed discovery. False confidence from GNU timeout : I initially ran the node under timeout -s INT 5 and treated exit code 124 as proof of clean operation. However, GNU timeout returns 124 whenever the time expires, regardless of whether the child process handled SIGINT cleanly or hung. I switched to launching in the background, issuing kill -INT, and checking the child’s actual exit status. The SIGINT shutdown crash : The actual exit status turned out to be 1. In ROS 2 Jazzy, rclpy.spin() raises ExternalShutdownException upon SIGINT. My finally: block was calling rclpy.shutdown() unconditionally on a context that had already been shut down, throwing an RCLError via pybind11. The fix was catching ExternalShutdownException and guarding if rclpy.ok(): rclpy.shutdown(). Swallowed tick exceptions : Wrapping the control loop in except Exception: and publishing zero commands masked runtime failures during CI smoke testing. The step now inspects the log to fail the build if any “Tick exception” occurred, and the node now latches fail-closed. Sensor beam count mismatch : The Webots TIAGo lidar outputs 667 samples, while a physical Hokuyo URG-04LX outputs 682. My first iteration auto-configured the gate parameters from the first scan received—which made length validation useless because it compared the scan against itself. Geometry parameters are now immutable at startup, and mismatched scans are discarded (TRIP_SENSOR_INVALID). Where this sits This supervisory gate is the physical foundation (Layer 1) of a broader research framework. A text-based moral filter (SEMEV-12) and a values-based action ranker (QERRA-THRIVE) sit upstream in deliberation; they are purely advisory and do not form part of the safety function. Repository & Documentation: GitHub - marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical: Three-layer deterministic safety & ethical execution guard for autonomous robots (ROS 2 & Behavior Trees). Sub-ms physical reflex (QERRA-HSR) + moral filter (SEMEV-12) + values ranker (THRIVE). Fully auditable. · GitHub Complete README: QERRA-v2-classical/README.md at main · marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical · GitHub Questions for the Community Bounding reaction latency : How do you measure and bound worst-case end-to-end reaction time in ROS 2 (sensor packet arrival → executor dispatch → supervisor decision → base controller command)? Is ros2_tracing the standard tool for this, and what instrumentation points would you recommend? Integration topology : For safety gatekeepers on /cmd_vel_safe, do you prefer direct topic remapping to the motor base, or integrating the supervisor into a twist_mux priority hierarchy? Lifecycle node management : Should a supervisory gate of this type be structured as a LifecycleNode? If so, how do you model a persistent “fault latched until restart” state without an external lifecycle manager inadvertently resetting the node before inspection? Benchmarking with nav2_collision_monitor : What would a fair, reproducible evaluation between a Simplex-style state machine and nav2_collision_monitor look like (e.g., standard bag replays, deceleration envelope metrics)? I built this with AI coding assistance (documented in the README) and verified every claim against test suites (192 unit tests passing) and CI logs. If you spot an error, architectural blind spot, or flawed assumption, please let me know. items.summary: Hi ROS community! Ever had two ROS 2 systems that could ping each other, use the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID , but still couldn’t discover each other’s topics? I’ve encountered similar issues while working with distributed ROS 2 systems. Troubleshooting often means manually investigating DDS discovery, middleware configurations, QoS policies, and container networking. To make this process more systematic, I developed DDS AutoDiag v0.1.0, an independent, MIT-licensed open-source tool for diagnosing ROS 2 communication problems across robots, computers, and containers. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. items.title: dbreunig/nesformer
items.summary: dbreunig/nesformer Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen! In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. Followed by: I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. How VicOne helps expose cyber risks in AI robot safeguards VicOne 27 Oct 2026 5 min read VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. A robot can follow its safety rules and still act on manipulated information. See what this means for robot safety and how teams can strengthen their testing and evidence. VicOne This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions. Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models , a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did. In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack. VicOne Safety-related decisions have inputs too An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated? At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved. A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes . The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall. Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information. Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm. VicOne Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed. Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research , a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once. Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated. Security testing strengthens robot safety evidence Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated. That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots . IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems . The EU Machinery Regulation , which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team. VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community , VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. VicOne’s Radeis helps teams validate potential effects before deployment, while Rthena provides visibility into risks and behavior during operation. Five questions safety and security teams should answer together The central test is whether a robot’s safeguards still protect people when the information they rely on is manipulated. Safety and security teams can begin by tracing the inputs behind each protective decision, challenging them, and revisiting the evidence as the robot changes. They can start with these five questions: 1. What does each protective function read? Map the readings, estimates, messages, and confirmations. Identify which safeguards operate independently of the robot’s AI decisions. 2. How does that information arrive? Check how inputs are produced, transmitted, authenticated where appropriate, and handled when they are missing or implausible. 3. What happens if an input is manipulated? Test false distances, drifting position estimates, and other relevant scenarios against the robot’s safety limits. 4. Can one action mislead several inputs? Check whether sensor fusion or seemingly independent safeguards share a point of failure. 5. When should the evidence be revisited? Reassess after changes to software, models, sensors, or operating conditions. Agree on bounded responses to suspicious behavior with the safety team in advance. The goal is not only to show that a protective function works. Teams also need evidence that it remains protective when the information behind its decision is wrong or deliberately manipulated — and that another safeguard can catch the resulting hazard when needed. As robots change, that evidence needs to change with them. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments. items.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics
items.summary: VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. The post 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, watch for VicOne’s upcoming white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .” Sponsored content by VicOne Tell Us What You Think! items.title: Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier
items.summary: To prove its commercial value, physical AI must get past funding enthusiasm and move into production environments. The post Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Genesis AI recently unveiled the Eno robot to bring physical AI into commercial environments. Source: Genesis AI The fastest-growing market categories have humble beginnings. Physical AI, the combination of robotics and advanced artificial intelligence, is just the latest example. ChatGPT began as a pitch deck at an accelerator before it became a household name in 2023. Before cloud computing became a boardroom imperative, founders were building it, server rack by server rack, cluster by cluster. And, of course, before fintech rewired retail banking, it appeared as a funding surge in deal flow data that most banks weren’t reading. You see the pattern, and I’ve watched it repeat itself across several years of evaluating startups. The startup ecosystem is the world’s most underutilized business intelligence system. Incumbents may amass wealth and power, but it’s the founders who choose to build. Which sectors attract a sudden surge of founding activity is a three-to-five-year leading indicator of where enterprise disruption is headed. While AI agents garner the lion’s share of media attention and VC funding , deal flow suggests the next market for hypergrowth will be of the metallic persuasion. That is physical AI , which includes autonomous machines and smart manufacturing, among other sensor-laden systems. Robotics and physical AI startups raised a record $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, or more than double the prior year, according to PitchBook. Genesis AI , which emerged from stealth with a $105 million seed round , recently demonstrated a wheeled robot that can bring physical AI into commercially relevant environments without needing to replicate the human body. Physical AI: Intelligence inside Physical AI systems can perceive environments, understand spatial context, make operational decisions, and act autonomously in real time across industrial and other settings. Physical AI systems move beyond static automation toward adaptive operations that continuously improve through interaction with the real world. As with most tech trends, physical AI is driven by a coalescence of several technologies that have matured simultaneously. These include: multimodal sensing , edge computing, simulation environments, robotics foundation models, and world modeling systems. These technologies allow machines to collect information from the physical environment, interpret it in context, simulate outcomes before acting, and continuously refine performance through operational feedback loops. In addition, the costs of several components that make physical AI possible have declined, with lidar , actuators , depth cameras , and sensors becoming more affordable. For example, Waymo said its sixth-generation Driver system significantly reduced costs while increasing resolution, range, and compute power. The autonomous vehicle system used a suite of 13 cameras, four lidars, and six radars . Together, the technological maturation plus cost reduction cultivates the right conditions for physical AI to blossom. Manufacturing , automotive , logistics , and healthcare sectors have emerged as major areas of capital concentration, with organizations actively piloting robotics to address labor costs and the scarcity of qualified personnel, and deploying them in harsh environments even as productivity needs grow. Figure AI , whose humanoid robots assemble automobile parts in BMW factories, reached a $39 billion valuation within three years, the fastest path to unicorn status in robotics history. Investors are banking on general-purpose robot models doing for hardware what large-language models did for software. Why wouldn’t they? The deal flow is there. Three stages of a disruption wave Throughout the past few years of reading deal flow, I’ve identified a consistent three-stage pattern that plays out across every major technology disruption. Stage 1: The founder surge A new capability emerges, attracting a disproportionate number of high-quality founding teams. Capital concentrates. Failure rates soar even as the survivors are defining the category. As I alluded to earlier, generative AI shot to the stars in 2023. Agentic AI is now moving through this stage, while physical AI is just entering it. Dyna Robotics , which is building foundation models that let one robot learn service tasks for hotels, restaurants, and laundromats, raised a $120 million Series A funding round within about a year of its founding. Stage 2: The corporate adoption wall Enterprises begin piloting the technology but struggle to move from experiment to production. The startups that survive stage one hit procurement cycles, integration complexity, and organizational resistance. We’re seeing this right now with organizations implementing GenAI and agentic AI tools without adapting their operating models, according to Deloitte. Some organizations break through this wall. After recognizing that generative AI would fundamentally reshape customer service, Intercom canceled non-AI projects, reorganized product teams and committed $100 million to replatform the business around AI. That transformation produced its Fin agent which now resolves millions of customer service queries. Another company, Maven Robotics , mixed palletizing in warehouses, and is crossing the wall one customer at a time. Stage 3: Industrialization A subset of companies cracks the deployment code. The technology becomes operational infrastructure. The window for competitive entry is closing. Cloud computing reached this stage around 2015. GenAI and agentic AI will land there within 18 to 24 months, as organizations redesign their processes and double down on their change management practices. Kiva Systems ‘ warehouse robots, bought by Amazon in 2012, grew into a fleet of more than 1 million. What was once a startup capability is now sophisticated infrastructure that new entrants can’t easily match. The practical implication is straightforward: by the time a technology reaches Stage 3, the structural advantages of early deployers are largely locked in. The companies that used AWS in 2010 to save money eventually built strong engineering cultures, data architectures, and product velocity in the ensuing years. Submit your innovation now! Physical AI today, something else tomorrow The same dynamic is playing out in AI today and the deal flow is telling us exactly which categories are where on that curve. For physical AI, the competitive advantage lies in the ability to build continuous operational learning loops where physical interaction generates data, data improves simulation and models, and improved models enhance real-world performance. As the deployment of these intelligent systems scales, they compound advantages through infrastructure integration , operational feedback and real-world learning. More data, operationalized appropriately, yields better outcomes. Most corporate leaders treat startup deal flow as noise. They may discount it as too early-stage, too speculative, or too distant from their operating reality. But rather than watch startup deal flow to find your next vendor, watch it to understand where the next generation of your competitive environment is being built. Then calibrate your own development and strategic roadmap accordingly. The signals are there; you just need to know how to read them. About the author Janis Skriveris is a principal and Plug and Play Ventures and director of its Deeptech Platform. He sources, diligences, and leads investments in deeptech and AI companies shaping the next generation of industrial and urban systems. Skriveris focuses on applied AI, robotics and autonomy, next-gen mobility, industrial technologies, and the built environment — real estate, construction, and infrastructure. He helps companies validate commercial traction, refine their go-to market strategies, and access Plug and Play’s global corporate network. Since 2017, Skriveris has led 37 investments, including unicorn Einride . Prior to Plug and Play, Skriveris worked at EY’s Assurance and Consulting Department, where he developed a deep understanding of various industries and honed his skills in strategic planning, risk management, and business transformation. He holds a bachelor’s degree in economics and entrepreneurship, graduating with distinction from the University of Latvia. items.title: Solving the Interconnect Challenge in Modern Robotics: How 3M Is Engineering for Motion, Density, and Uptime
items.summary: As robotics systems grow more capable — faster, more precise, and increasingly reliant on AI-driven vision and control — the humble interconnect is being asked to do more than ever. The post Solving the Interconnect Challenge in Modern Robotics: How 3M Is Engineering for Motion, Density, and Uptime appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: By Heilind Electronics As robotics systems grow more capable — faster, more precise, and increasingly reliant on AI-driven vision and control — the humble interconnect is being asked to do more than ever. Signal integrity, mechanical durability, and board real estate are no longer secondary considerations in robotics design; they’re often the limiting factor. 3M has built out a portfolio of connectors, cables, and cable assemblies aimed squarely at these pressure points, and the company’s interconnect strategy for robotics offers a useful lens into where the industry’s hardware challenges are heading. Flex Life Is the New Uptime Metric Robotic joints, arms, and end effectors don’t sit still — they twist, bend, and cycle continuously, often for years without a maintenance window. Cabling that fatigues or fails under that mechanical stress is one of the more common causes of unplanned downtime in automated systems. 3M’s answer is a family of high-flex cable assemblies built specifically for motion-intensive applications. CoaXPress-compatible assemblies are flex-cycle tested to 45 million cycles, while USB3 Vision-compatible assemblies push that rating to 100 million cycles. On the flat-ribbon side — used widely for I/O and data runs in robotic subsystems — 3M offers a range spanning roughly 1 million to 100 million flex cycles, giving engineers a way to match cable durability to the actual duty cycle of a given axis or joint, rather than over- or under-engineering the harness. For machine vision applications specifically, where camera cables are constantly routed through moving linkages, this kind of validated flex-life data lets designers make a real engineering trade-off instead of a guess. IDC Termination: An Old Idea Still Solving New Problems 3M invented Insulation Displacement Contact (IDC) termination back in 1961, and it remains one of the more underappreciated tools in high-mix robotics manufacturing. Rather than crimping or soldering individual conductors, IDC connectors displace the wire insulation during a single mass-termination step; 3M IDC solutions can save up to 80% in wiring time compared with crimp-style connectors. That speed advantage compounds in two directions that matter to robotics builders. On the production floor, IDC simplifies mass termination across ribbon cable and multi-conductor harnesses, which is particularly relevant given how much I/O and sensor wiring modern robots carry. In the field, many IDC-based connectors support one-hand mating and unmating, which shortens service windows when a module needs to be swapped on a production line that can’t afford extended downtime. Board Space Is Getting More Expensive As robotic controllers and sensor modules pack more compute and I/O into the same footprint, connector real estate has become a genuine design constraint. 3M’s response includes reduced-pitch options like the Cable Socket 451 and Header 452 Series, built at half the pitch of the industry-standard 0.100-inch grid — effectively doubling contact density in the same board area. For lower pin-count applications — 2- to 4-wire sensor and signal connections that are ubiquitous in robotics — 3M’s Mini-Clamp connectors offer a compact footprint without requiring a full IDC harness, while the Mini Stack header and socket family pushes board footprint reduction even further for designs where every square millimeter counts. Reliability Under Vibration and Noise Constant motion brings constant vibration, and vibration is what turns a marginal connection into an intermittent fault. Several of 3M’s connector lines incorporate screw-lock retention specifically to maintain contact integrity in environments where mechanical disturbance is the norm rather than the exception. EMI and crosstalk are the other reliability variable in dense robotic wiring, where high-speed data lines often run in close proximity to motor and power cabling. 3M offers cable and connector options selected specifically to help manage that interference, which matters increasingly as robots incorporate more real-time vision and sensor fusion. For applications that need a sealed, one-piece solution rather than a discrete connector-and-cable assembly, 3M’s Molded-On Cable Assemblies provide a ruggedized, fully customizable option — useful where a robot’s environment (washdown, particulate, or extreme vibration) makes a traditional connector interface a liability. Why This Matters for Robotics Engineers Flex-tested cables, IDC termination, and reduced-pitch connectors represent the kinds of infrastructure decisions that can influence a robotics platform’s reliability and performance in the field. As robotic systems take on more autonomous, safety-critical, and continuously operating roles, the interconnects tying sensors to controllers to actuators become a real point of engineering leverage rather than an afterthought. 3M’s robotics-focused interconnect lineup, including high-flex cable assemblies, IDC connectors, reduced-pitch board connectors, and molded cable assemblies, gives design engineers a menu of validated options for addressing flex life, assembly time, board density, and long-term reliability. For teams building or specifying the next generation of robotic hardware, that combination of decades of interconnect experience and application-specific testing (like the 45- and 100-million-cycle flex ratings) is worth a closer look during the component selection phase, well before a design freeze locks those decisions in. items.summary: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents […]
items.articleText: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument. Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours. Science Fact, Not Fiction The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula. Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon. items.articleText: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. entries.title: dbreunig/nesformer: Qwen3.5-4B 가중치에 통합된 NES 6502 CPU 에뮬레이터
entries.reason: LLM 가중치 내에 하드웨어 CPU 로직을 내장하여 추론 과정에서 ROM 코드를 직접 연산·실행하는 실험적 사례를 다룹니다.

facts.statement: Drew Breunig가 Qwen3.5-4B 모델 가중치에 닌텐도 6502 CPU 에뮬레이터를 내장하여 모델 추론을 통해 NES 게임 ROM을 실행하는 nesformer 프로젝트를 공개했습니다.
facts.quote: Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B.

entries.title: VicOne, AI 지원 연구로 피지컬 AI 도구에서 28개 제로데이 취약점 발견
entries.reason: 로봇 학습 및 시뮬레이션 환경에 쓰이는 주요 소프트웨어의 제로데이 취약점이 로봇 안전과 검증 신뢰도에 미칠 수 있는 위험을 다룹니다.

facts.statement: VicOne 연구진은 Google, NVIDIA, Meta 등이 관리하는 피지컬 AI 생태계 지원 도구에서 AI 지원 연구를 통해 28건의 제로데이 취약점을 식별했다고 발표했습니다.
facts.quote: VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem.

entries.title: PitchBook 집계, 2025년 피지컬 AI 및 로보틱스 투자 유치 276억 달러 기록
entries.reason: 자율 기계 및 스마트 제조 분야 스타트업으로 유입되는 글로벌 투자 규모와 피지컬 AI 상용화 단계의 자본 흐름을 전달합니다.

facts.statement: PitchBook 집계에 따르면 2025년 로보틱스 및 피지컬 AI 스타트업이 1,009건의 거래를 통해 전년 대비 2배 이상인 총 276억 달러의 투자를 유치했습니다.
facts.quote: Robotics and physical AI startups raised a record $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, or more than double the prior year, according to PitchBook.

entries.title: NVIDIA Omniverse 및 AI 에이전트를 결합한 로보틱스 시뮬레이션 워크플로
entries.reason: GPT-6 Astra 등 AI 에이전트와 Isaac Sim/Omniverse 라이브러리를 연동해 로봇 조작, 케이블 배선, 대규모 물류창고 시뮬레이션을 생성·검증하는 실무 사례를 소개합니다.

facts.statement: 개발자들이 대형 언어 모델 에이전트와 NVIDIA Omniverse 및 Isaac Sim 라이브러리를 결합하여 건물 모델 재구성, 케이블 배선 조작, 물류창고 성능 스트레스 테스트 등 로봇 시뮬레이션을 구축하는 방식을 공개했습니다.
facts.quote: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended.

omitted.reason: 컨퍼런스 통역 서비스 이용 후기를 묻는 단순 커뮤니티 의견 수렴 글로 기술 개발 관련 정보가 없음.
릴리스 번호 외에 구체적인 기능 변경이나 사용 조건에 대한 기술적 설명이 없는 단순 버전 태그임.
세부적인 기술 변경 내역이나 개발 관련 정보가 없는 짧은 피드 요약임.
AI 학습 공정 이용(fair use)과 관련된 법원 제출 의견서 발췌 요약으로 제품·기술 소식이나 구체적인 산업 실행 사항이 아님.
LLM 도입이 문서 및 소프트웨어 신뢰도에 미치는 영향에 대한 블로그 인용구로 구체적인 기술 릴리스가 아님.
알파(alpha) 단계의 프리릴리스 버전이며 중요한 호환성 변경이나 지원 종료 예고에 해당하지 않음.
여러 로봇 비디오와 행사 일정을 취합한 주간 큐레이션 글로 개별 기술의 구체적인 개발·릴리스 근거가 부족함.
사이버 보안 백서 홍보를 위한 스폰서 기사로 개념적 설명 위주이며 독립적인 기술 릴리스나 제품 업데이트가 아님.
부품 유통사의 협찬 홍보성 기사로 일반적인 커넥터 제품군 소개 및 마케팅 내용 위주임.
외계 전파 신호 탐색을 위한 천문 관측 프로젝트 소개로 로보틱스 및 범용 AI 개발 도구와의 직접적인 연관성이 부족함.

draft.one_sentence_summary: ROS 2 및 Gazebo 기반 도구 공개, LLM 가중치 연산 및 샌드박스 취약점 분석, 피지컬 AI 투자 규모 집계가 발표되었습니다.
draft.section_robotics:
- **livox_gz_sim**: Gazebo Harmonic 환경에서 CUDA 종속성 없이 Livox Mid-360 및 HAP 라이다의 비반복 스캔 패턴과 IMU를 모사하는 오픈소스 시뮬레이션 플러그인이 공개되었습니다 [1].
- **qerra_core**: 상위 속도 명령과 베이스 제어기 사이에서 충돌 방지 및 안전 정지를 결정론적으로 제어하는 ROS 2 Jazzy 지원 패키지 qerra_core 0.3.0이 시뮬레이션 및 CI 검증과 함께 공개되었습니다 [2].
- **DDS AutoDiag**: ROS 2 통신의 DDS 탐색, 네트워크 구성, QoS 호환성 등 23가지 항목을 점검하고 자연어 기반 RViz 설정 및 AI 진단을 지원하는 오픈소스 도구 DDS AutoDiag v0.1.0이 출시되었습니다 [4].
- **Omniverse 기반 로보틱스 워크플로**: 대형 언어 모델 에이전트와 NVIDIA Omniverse 및 Isaac Sim 라이브러리를 연동해 건물 모델 재구성, 케이블 조작, 물류창고 부하 테스트 등 로봇 시뮬레이션 환경을 구축하는 사례가 소개되었습니다 [19].
draft.section_devtools:
- **ChatGPT HTML 샌드박스 취약점**: Parameter Labs는 ChatGPT의 HTML 미리보기 샌드박스 환경에서 MathLive 라이브러리와 innerHTML 처리를 악용해 사용자 계정 권한 및 데이터를 탈취할 수 있는 취약점을 보고했습니다 [10].
- **nesformer**: Qwen3.5-4B 모델 가중치 내에 닌텐도 6502 CPU 에뮬레이터를 내장하여 모델 추론 과정에서 NES 게임 ROM을 직접 연산·실행하는 실험적 프로젝트가 공개되었습니다 [12].
draft.section_industry:
- **OpenAI 웹 학습 방침**: OpenAI는 웹사이트 운영자가 AI 모델 학습 참여 여부 및 선호도를 표준화된 방식으로 전달할 수 있도록 공유 robots.txt 신호를 준수할 방침임을 밝혔습니다 [6].
- **VicOne 취약점 분석**: VicOne 연구진은 Google, NVIDIA, Meta 등이 관리하는 피지컬 AI 생태계 지원 도구에서 AI 지원 연구를 통해 28건의 제로데이 취약점을 식별했다고 발표했습니다 [15].
- **PitchBook 피지컬 AI 투자 집계**: PitchBook 집계에 따르면 2025년 글로벌 로보틱스 및 피지컬 AI 스타트업이 총 1,009건의 거래를 통해 전년 대비 2배 이상인 276억 달러의 투자를 유치했습니다 [16].

findings: 초안의 사실 관계, 한정 조건, 인용 번호 보존 상태를 확인했습니다.
초안에서 공란이었던 교차 관찰(cross_insight)에 qerra_core[2]와 VicOne 취약점 분석[15]을 연결한 해석을 보완했습니다.

selectedItems.summary: Hi all, I’ve released livox_gz_sim, a Gazebo Harmonic plugin that simulates Livox Mid-360 and HAP lidars and publishes exactly what livox_ros_driver2 publishes. As far as I know it’s the first gpu agnostic Livox simulator for Gazebo Harmonic; the existing ones target Gazebo Classic or require CUDA. What it does Uses Livox’s recorded non-repetitive scan patterns, so coverage builds up over frames like on the real sensor Publishes livox_ros_driver2/CustomMsg or PointCloud2 in the driver’s 26-byte layout (xfer_format 0/1), with per-point timestamps Simulates the Mid-360’s IMU at 200 Hz Adds range and angle noise from the datasheet, and reflectivity (0–255) from <laser_retro> Supports multiple sensors, configurable publish rate and downsampling, and world resets Because the output matches the driver, stacks like FAST-LIO run on it unchanged. selectedItems.articleText: A small deterministic gate between the planner and the wheels: ROS 2 Jazzy node, simulation and CI only - Projects - Open Robotics Discourse A small deterministic gate between the planner and the wheels: ROS 2 Jazzy node, simulation and CI only Projects ros2 , jazzy , supervisorygate marunigno-ship-it November 1, 2026, 11:04am 1 I’ve been building a small supervisor node for differential-drive mobile robots that sits between a high-level velocity source (such as Nav2, an LLM agent, or teleoperation) and the base controller. Following the classic Simplex architecture (Sha et al.), the node treats complex high-level planners as unverified proposers and acts as a minimal, deterministic gatekeeper on /cmd_vel. I work alone and I’m self-taught, based in Greece. I have no access to physical robot hardware, so everything described below is evaluated in Webots simulation (PAL Robotics TIAGo base) and verified in GitHub Actions Linux containers. I want to share what the node does, what the CI shows and doesn’t show, and the specific mistakes I made getting it through CI, in the hope it saves someone else an afternoon, or not What it is The package is qerra_core (node qerra_gate_node, version 0.3.0, Apache-2.0, ROS 2 Jazzy). It subscribes to /cmd_vel, /scan, and an operator reset topic, and publishes /cmd_vel_safe and diagnostic JSON on /gate/state. planner (Nav2, teleop, etc.) --/cmd_vel–> [ qerra_gate_node ] --/cmd_vel_safe–> base controller /scan ------^ distress input (UDP 5008) --^ The core decision logic is a pure function—step(state, params, inputs)—implemented using standard-library integer arithmetic with no external dependencies and with timestamps passed in as inputs. This design allows control cycles to be replayed and verified offline bit-for-bit. Key behaviors: Kinematic stopping envelope : Clamps wheel velocity commands against a swept forward lidar corridor: d_stop = ceil(v^2 / (2*a)) + ceil(v * t_react) + margin (where a = 0.5 m/s², t_react = 32 ms, margin = 300 mm). Fail-closed trips : Commands zero velocity and latches on obstacle breach, stale/invalid proposals (≥ 150 ms), sensor stalls, or acute distress telemetry. Calm dwell & operator reset : Once tripped, the robot remains stationary. Resuming motion strictly requires a continuous 1.0-second clear dwell window followed by an explicit operator reset message (/gate/reset). Reset is strictly refused while a hazard is present. Distress reflex input (Layer 1B) : Ingests non-blocking UDP telemetry (port 5008) inspired by ISO 13482 assistive cobot principles, tripping the gate on CRITICAL distress. (“HSR” in my documentation is my internal project name for this reflex layer and has no connection to Toyota’s robot). Node-level fault latch : If an unhandled exception occurs inside the 32 ms control tick, the node latches into a permanent FAULT state, continually publishes a zero velocity command, reports the fault reason over /gate/state, and refuses to move until the process is restarted. Topology note : The base controller is intended to be wired to /cmd_vel_safe, and nothing else should publish to it. ROS 2 topic namespaces do not enforce sole write authority. What I can show (The Evidence) Simulation replays : Webots runs logging each tick with a SHA-256 rolling hash chain that verifies offline via verify_log.py --replay. In Demo 7, an obstacle trip fired at 337 mm clearance, reaching standstill at 301 mm (36 mm coasting). In Demo 9, injected human distress tripped the gate within the same 32 ms tick (cycle 125), held standstill through dwell stabilization, and motion resumed only after an authorized reset. Native ROS 2 Jazzy CI (workflow file: QERRA-v2-classical/.github/workflows/ros2_jazzy.yml at main · marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical · GitHub Running on Ubuntu 24.04 in an official ros:jazzy container, GitHub Actions builds the package with colcon, verifies discovery in lib/qerra_core, starts the executable from a neutral directory (/tmp), captures a live /gate/state message, sends SIGINT, and strictly asserts that the process exits with code 0 and logs zero tick exceptions. What I cannot show (Honesty Boundaries) No hardware validation : Everything is simulation and CI. A 0.0 velocity command is a software setpoint delivered to motor drivers, not a certified hardware Safe Torque Off (STO), brake coil, or emergency stop. If the gate process dies, the base controller will maintain its last command unless the base has its own hardware or software command timeout. Timing and jitter : The node runs on a Python timer at 31.25 Hz on general-purpose Linux. I have not profiled execution jitter under heavy system load. Reaction time (t_react) : The 32 ms figure is a simulation assumption. On a real robot, total reaction latency includes physical sensor scan time (a Hokuyo URG-04LX operates at ~10 Hz / 100 ms), executor queueing, DDS transport, and motor deceleration ramps. Until measured, d_stop is likely optimistic for real hardware. Comparison with Nav2 : I have not benchmarked this against nav2_collision_monitor. nav2_collision_monitor is far more mature and feature-complete. My implementation is an exploration of Simplex state-latching, explicit calm dwells, and replayable pure-function cores. Standards are informative : References to ISO 13849-1, ISO 13482, and ISO 3691-4 are conceptual references only; no formal compliance is claimed. What went wrong in CI (Lessons Learned) Getting the standalone node to build, tick, and terminate cleanly under native Jazzy CI exposed five subtle issues: Missing setup.cfg : The console script was initially installed into bin/ rather than lib//, leaving ros2 pkg executables completely blank. Adding setup.cfg with explicit script directories fixed discovery. False confidence from GNU timeout : I initially ran the node under timeout -s INT 5 and treated exit code 124 as proof of clean operation. However, GNU timeout returns 124 whenever the time expires, regardless of whether the child process handled SIGINT cleanly or hung. I switched to launching in the background, issuing kill -INT, and checking the child’s actual exit status. The SIGINT shutdown crash : The actual exit status turned out to be 1. In ROS 2 Jazzy, rclpy.spin() raises ExternalShutdownException upon SIGINT. My finally: block was calling rclpy.shutdown() unconditionally on a context that had already been shut down, throwing an RCLError via pybind11. The fix was catching ExternalShutdownException and guarding if rclpy.ok(): rclpy.shutdown(). Swallowed tick exceptions : Wrapping the control loop in except Exception: and publishing zero commands masked runtime failures during CI smoke testing. The step now inspects the log to fail the build if any “Tick exception” occurred, and the node now latches fail-closed. Sensor beam count mismatch : The Webots TIAGo lidar outputs 667 samples, while a physical Hokuyo URG-04LX outputs 682. My first iteration auto-configured the gate parameters from the first scan received—which made length validation useless because it compared the scan against itself. Geometry parameters are now immutable at startup, and mismatched scans are discarded (TRIP_SENSOR_INVALID). Where this sits This supervisory gate is the physical foundation (Layer 1) of a broader research framework. A text-based moral filter (SEMEV-12) and a values-based action ranker (QERRA-THRIVE) sit upstream in deliberation; they are purely advisory and do not form part of the safety function. Repository & Documentation: GitHub - marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical: Three-layer deterministic safety & ethical execution guard for autonomous robots (ROS 2 & Behavior Trees). Sub-ms physical reflex (QERRA-HSR) + moral filter (SEMEV-12) + values ranker (THRIVE). Fully auditable. · GitHub Complete README: QERRA-v2-classical/README.md at main · marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical · GitHub Questions for the Community Bounding reaction latency : How do you measure and bound worst-case end-to-end reaction time in ROS 2 (sensor packet arrival → executor dispatch → supervisor decision → base controller command)? Is ros2_tracing the standard tool for this, and what instrumentation points would you recommend? Integration topology : For safety gatekeepers on /cmd_vel_safe, do you prefer direct topic remapping to the motor base, or integrating the supervisor into a twist_mux priority hierarchy? Lifecycle node management : Should a supervisory gate of this type be structured as a LifecycleNode? If so, how do you model a persistent “fault latched until restart” state without an external lifecycle manager inadvertently resetting the node before inspection? Benchmarking with nav2_collision_monitor : What would a fair, reproducible evaluation between a Simplex-style state machine and nav2_collision_monitor look like (e.g., standard bag replays, deceleration envelope metrics)?
