selectedItems.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics
selectedItems.summary: VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. The post 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, watch for VicOne’s upcoming white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .” Sponsored content by VicOne Tell Us What You Think! selectedItems.title: Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier
selectedItems.summary: To prove its commercial value, physical AI must get past funding enthusiasm and move into production environments. The post Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: Genesis AI recently unveiled the Eno robot to bring physical AI into commercial environments. Source: Genesis AI The fastest-growing market categories have humble beginnings. Physical AI, the combination of robotics and advanced artificial intelligence, is just the latest example. ChatGPT began as a pitch deck at an accelerator before it became a household name in 2023. Before cloud computing became a boardroom imperative, founders were building it, server rack by server rack, cluster by cluster. And, of course, before fintech rewired retail banking, it appeared as a funding surge in deal flow data that most banks weren’t reading. You see the pattern, and I’ve watched it repeat itself across several years of evaluating startups. The startup ecosystem is the world’s most underutilized business intelligence system. Incumbents may amass wealth and power, but it’s the founders who choose to build. Which sectors attract a sudden surge of founding activity is a three-to-five-year leading indicator of where enterprise disruption is headed. While AI agents garner the lion’s share of media attention and VC funding , deal flow suggests the next market for hypergrowth will be of the metallic persuasion. That is physical AI , which includes autonomous machines and smart manufacturing, among other sensor-laden systems. Robotics and physical AI startups raised a record $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, or more than double the prior year, according to PitchBook. Genesis AI , which emerged from stealth with a $105 million seed round , recently demonstrated a wheeled robot that can bring physical AI into commercially relevant environments without needing to replicate the human body. Physical AI: Intelligence inside Physical AI systems can perceive environments, understand spatial context, make operational decisions, and act autonomously in real time across industrial and other settings. Physical AI systems move beyond static automation toward adaptive operations that continuously improve through interaction with the real world. As with most tech trends, physical AI is driven by a coalescence of several technologies that have matured simultaneously. These include: multimodal sensing , edge computing, simulation environments, robotics foundation models, and world modeling systems. These technologies allow machines to collect information from the physical environment, interpret it in context, simulate outcomes before acting, and continuously refine performance through operational feedback loops. In addition, the costs of several components that make physical AI possible have declined, with lidar , actuators , depth cameras , and sensors becoming more affordable. For example, Waymo said its sixth-generation Driver system significantly reduced costs while increasing resolution, range, and compute power. The autonomous vehicle system used a suite of 13 cameras, four lidars, and six radars . Together, the technological maturation plus cost reduction cultivates the right conditions for physical AI to blossom. Manufacturing , automotive , logistics , and healthcare sectors have emerged as major areas of capital concentration, with organizations actively piloting robotics to address labor costs and the scarcity of qualified personnel, and deploying them in harsh environments even as productivity needs grow. Figure AI , whose humanoid robots assemble automobile parts in BMW factories, reached a $39 billion valuation within three years, the fastest path to unicorn status in robotics history. Investors are banking on general-purpose robot models doing for hardware what large-language models did for software. Why wouldn’t they? The deal flow is there. Three stages of a disruption wave Throughout the past few years of reading deal flow, I’ve identified a consistent three-stage pattern that plays out across every major technology disruption. Stage 1: The founder surge A new capability emerges, attracting a disproportionate number of high-quality founding teams. Capital concentrates. Failure rates soar even as the survivors are defining the category. As I alluded to earlier, generative AI shot to the stars in 2023. Agentic AI is now moving through this stage, while physical AI is just entering it. Dyna Robotics , which is building foundation models that let one robot learn service tasks for hotels, restaurants, and laundromats, raised a $120 million Series A funding round within about a year of its founding. Stage 2: The corporate adoption wall Enterprises begin piloting the technology but struggle to move from experiment to production. The startups that survive stage one hit procurement cycles, integration complexity, and organizational resistance. We’re seeing this right now with organizations implementing GenAI and agentic AI tools without adapting their operating models, according to Deloitte. Some organizations break through this wall. After recognizing that generative AI would fundamentally reshape customer service, Intercom canceled non-AI projects, reorganized product teams and committed $100 million to replatform the business around AI. That transformation produced its Fin agent which now resolves millions of customer service queries. Another company, Maven Robotics , mixed palletizing in warehouses, and is crossing the wall one customer at a time. Stage 3: Industrialization A subset of companies cracks the deployment code. The technology becomes operational infrastructure. The window for competitive entry is closing. Cloud computing reached this stage around 2015. GenAI and agentic AI will land there within 18 to 24 months, as organizations redesign their processes and double down on their change management practices. Kiva Systems ‘ warehouse robots, bought by Amazon in 2012, grew into a fleet of more than 1 million. What was once a startup capability is now sophisticated infrastructure that new entrants can’t easily match. The practical implication is straightforward: by the time a technology reaches Stage 3, the structural advantages of early deployers are largely locked in. The companies that used AWS in 2010 to save money eventually built strong engineering cultures, data architectures, and product velocity in the ensuing years. Submit your innovation now! Physical AI today, something else tomorrow The same dynamic is playing out in AI today and the deal flow is telling us exactly which categories are where on that curve. For physical AI, the competitive advantage lies in the ability to build continuous operational learning loops where physical interaction generates data, data improves simulation and models, and improved models enhance real-world performance. As the deployment of these intelligent systems scales, they compound advantages through infrastructure integration , operational feedback and real-world learning. More data, operationalized appropriately, yields better outcomes. Most corporate leaders treat startup deal flow as noise. They may discount it as too early-stage, too speculative, or too distant from their operating reality. But rather than watch startup deal flow to find your next vendor, watch it to understand where the next generation of your competitive environment is being built. Then calibrate your own development and strategic roadmap accordingly. The signals are there; you just need to know how to read them. About the author Janis Skriveris is a principal and Plug and Play Ventures and director of its Deeptech Platform. He sources, diligences, and leads investments in deeptech and AI companies shaping the next generation of industrial and urban systems. Skriveris focuses on applied AI, robotics and autonomy, next-gen mobility, industrial technologies, and the built environment — real estate, construction, and infrastructure. He helps companies validate commercial traction, refine their go-to market strategies, and access Plug and Play’s global corporate network. Since 2017, Skriveris has led 37 investments, including unicorn Einride . Prior to Plug and Play, Skriveris worked at EY’s Assurance and Consulting Department, where he developed a deep understanding of various industries and honed his skills in strategic planning, risk management, and business transformation. He holds a bachelor’s degree in economics and entrepreneurship, graduating with distinction from the University of Latvia. selectedItems.articleText: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion.
